summary:
Lunar Horizon is a browser tool for comparing lunar landing sites and landing dates. Pick a site and a date, and it shows where the Sun and Earth sit relative to the horizon, then reports what a mission would actually get: percentage of time in sunlight, percentage with a direct-to-Earth link, the longest unbroken night, the longest communications blackout, and the energy a solar array would collect.

The difference from a flat-map answer is the horizon. Near the lunar south pole the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees, so whether a site is lit depends on the terrain around it, not just its latitude. We walked the LOLA LDEM_75S_120M digital elevation model outward from each site in 360 directions to 100 km and built a measured skyline for every candidate below 79 degrees south. Sites are judged against that real profile instead of a smooth sphere.

That changes answers. Shackleton reads 100 percent sunlit against a sphere and 48 percent against its own crater rim. Mons Mouton keeps its sunlight across a full lunar day, but by only 0.43 degrees at the tightest moment, so the tool says so rather than printing a confident 100 percent.

The sky geometry is validated against JPL Horizons to 0.007 degrees. It runs entirely in the browser with no backend.
details:
What it does:

Lunar Horizon answers two questions for a lunar landing site: how much sunlight will a lander get, and how much of the time can it talk to Earth. You choose a site from a catalogue of 30 real candidates or enter your own coordinates, choose a landing date and a mission length from 24 hours to a year, and the tool computes the full mission.

It reports sunlight fraction, direct-to-Earth availability, the overlap between the two, longest night, longest communications blackout, and total collected energy per square metre. A 360-degree horizon view shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain silhouette. A chart plots both bodies through the mission. A slip table shows what happens if launch slides by a week or a lunar month.

How it works:

Sun and Earth vectors come from Astronomy Engine, rotated into the Mean Earth frame using the IAU lunar pole and prime meridian. Positions are airless and topocentric on the 1737.4 km datum sphere. We validated against JPL Horizons apparent azimuth and elevation across eight independent test cases covering polar, equatorial and far-side sites; the worst disagreement is 0.007 degrees.

The horizon is the part that matters. We processed LOLA LDEM_75S_120M, the polar digital elevation model at 120 m per pixel, walking great circles outward from each site to 100 km in 360 azimuth directions and keeping the highest elevation angle each ray reaches. That produces a measured skyline for the 17 catalogue sites south of 79 degrees. A body counts as visible when any part of its disk clears that skyline on its own bearing, which matters because at the pole Earth’s upper limb can be up while its centre is still below the horizon, and that one degree is the entire communications link.

Why it matters:

Near the south pole, terrain is the answer. Shackleton reports 100 percent sunlight against a smooth sphere and 48 percent against its own rim. The tool shows both numbers side by side so the difference is visible rather than hidden in an assumption.

It also refuses to oversell. Mons Mouton stays sunlit across a full lunar day, but the Sun’s lower limb comes within 0.43 degrees of the skyline at its worst moment, and a ridge finer than the DEM’s 120 m resolution would end it. The interface prints that margin and names the feature responsible. A thin margin is a question for a terrain study, not an answer.

Tools:

Vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS with no framework, no bundler and no backend. It opens by double-clicking a file. The Moon globe is a hand-drawn orthographic projection on a 2D canvas rather than WebGL, because a WebGL texture loaded from a local file is treated as cross-origin and cannot be used. Astronomy Engine supplies the ephemeris. The DEM was processed offline with Node.js scripts included in the repository. Basemap imagery is the NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit LROC WAC mosaic. Verification runs against the live JPL Horizons API.

Creativity:

Most landing-site tools give you a number. This one gives you the number and the margin, names the mountain that would take your sunlight away, and shows what you would have concluded without a DEM so you can see what the terrain changed.
